questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 7-year-old boy presents with a 3-week history of right-sided ear discharge, progressive hearing loss, and fever unresponsive to oral amoxicillin. On examination, there is post-auricular swelling with downward and forward displacement of the pinna, loss of post-auricular sulcus, and a sagging posterior superior canal wall. CT temporal bone shows a hypodense area with peripheral enhancement in the mastoid. The MOST appropriate next step in management is:

options.A: Oral ciprofloxacin for 4 weeks
options.B: IV ceftriaxone alone for 48 hours and reassess
options.C: Cortical mastoidectomy with IV antibiotics
options.D: Myringotomy and grommet insertion

questions.explanation: This is coalescent acute mastoiditis with subperiosteal abscess (post-auricular swelling, displaced pinna, sagging canal wall, CT hypodense lesion = pus). Management = surgical drainage via cortical mastoidectomy + IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone ± metronidazole). Option A: oral antibiotics inadequate for abscess. Option B: IV antibiotics alone insufficient once abscess forms — surgical drainage mandatory. Option D: myringotomy/grommet is for OME, not mastoid abscess. PEARL: Sagging of posterior superior canal wall = pathognomonic of coalescent mastoiditis requiring surgery.

questions.subject: ENT
key_findings: Soft tissue mass in Prussak's space (epitympanum)
Erosion of ossicular chain (incus long process)
Scutum erosion visible
Lateral epitympanic wall destruction
No fluid level — solid soft tissue density
questions.question_text: A 35-year-old man presents with foul-smelling right ear discharge for 8 years, progressive hearing loss, and a recent episode of vertigo. Otoscopy shows a pearly white mass with keratin debris in the attic region. HRCT temporal bone (image shown) demonstrates findings as described. Which of the following statements about this condition is CORRECT?

options.A: It arises from stratified squamous epithelium and is a true neoplasm
options.B: Pars tensa retraction pocket is the commonest route of acquired cholesteatoma formation
options.C: Attic perforation with pars flaccida retraction is the hallmark of acquired cholesteatoma
options.D: It can be safely managed with antibiotics and aural toilet long-term

questions.explanation: Acquired cholesteatoma (commonest type) arises from pars flaccida retraction pocket (Shrapnell's membrane) into Prussak's space → attic (epitympanic) location. Option A: Cholesteatoma is NOT a true neoplasm — it is a benign but locally destructive lesion of keratinizing squamous epithelium. Option B: Pars tensa perforation leads to sinus cholesteatoma (posterior type) — LESS common. Pars flaccida/attic route is commonest. Option D: Surgery (modified radical/canal wall-down mastoidectomy) is definitive — no medical cure. PEARL: Foul smell + attic crust + conductive hearing loss = cholesteatoma until proven otherwise. Danger: facial nerve palsy, labyrinthine fistula, meningitis, brain abscess.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 55-year-old woman complains of bilateral progressive hearing loss, worse in noisy environments, and tinnitus for 3 years. Tuning fork tests show Rinne positive bilaterally and Weber lateralizing to neither ear. Audiometry shows bilateral symmetrical high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss with a characteristic 4kHz dip. She worked in a textile mill for 25 years. Which additional finding is MOST expected on this audiogram?

options.A: Low-frequency (250–500 Hz) threshold elevation with recruitment
options.B: Carhart's notch at 2 kHz on bone conduction
options.C: Recovery of thresholds at 8 kHz beyond the 4 kHz notch
options.D: Type B tympanogram with absent stapedial reflexes

questions.explanation: Noise-induced hearing loss (NIHL) causes a characteristic 4 kHz notch on audiogram with partial recovery (improvement) at 8 kHz — the 'noise notch'. This differentiates it from presbycusis (which shows progressive slope downward without recovery). Option A: Low-frequency loss with recruitment = Meniere's disease. Option B: Carhart's notch at 2 kHz on BC = otosclerosis (mechanical artefact of reduced ossicular inertia). Option D: Type B tympanogram = OME (middle ear effusion, not sensorineural). PEARL: 4 kHz is maximally susceptible to noise damage because the cochlear region for 4 kHz is 9–10 mm from the oval window and is the area of maximum mechanical stress.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 28-year-old woman presents with bilateral progressive hearing loss worsening during pregnancy. She reports better hearing in noisy environments (paracusis Willisii). Examination shows a reddish hue through the tympanic membrane. Audiometry shows bilateral low-frequency conductive hearing loss. Which of the following BEST explains the pathophysiology of hearing improvement in noisy environments in this patient?

options.A: Noise causes stapedial reflex activation improving ossicular coupling
options.B: In noisy environments, speakers raise their voice amplitude, improving signal-to-noise ratio for the patient
options.C: Noise activates cochlear efferent fibers improving hair cell sensitivity
options.D: Low-frequency ambient noise masks tinnitus, improving speech comprehension

questions.explanation: Paracusis Willisii (Willis paracusis) in otosclerosis: In noisy environments, normal-hearing speakers unconsciously raise their voice; since the patient's inner ear is normal, they benefit more from the louder signal — they hear RELATIVELY better. Option A: Stapedial reflex cannot be activated — stapes is fixed (the key pathology in otosclerosis). Option C: Cochlear efferent activation (olivocochlear bundle) is not related to this phenomenon. Option D: Tinnitus masking is a separate concept. PEARL: Schwartze sign (flamingo pink blush) = active vascular otospongiosis. Carhart's notch (2 kHz BC notch) is mechanical artefact. Treatment: stapedectomy/stapedotomy.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 45-year-old woman presents with episodic vertigo lasting 20–30 minutes, left-sided low-frequency hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness. Symptoms began 2 years ago and are occurring more frequently. Audiometry shows left low-frequency SNHL. Glycerol dehydration test shows >15 dB improvement at low frequencies. Which of the following statements about this condition is MOST accurate?

options.A: Endolymphatic hydrops with rupture of Reissner's membrane is the underlying mechanism
options.B: High-frequency hearing loss is the earliest and most reliable audiometric marker
options.C: MRI always shows endolymphatic sac enlargement confirming diagnosis
options.D: Intratympanic gentamicin preserves hearing while controlling vertigo

questions.explanation: Meniere's disease = endolymphatic hydrops (excess endolymph). The classical explanation: when hydrops reaches critical pressure, Reissner's membrane ruptures → K+-rich endolymph mixes with perilymph → depolarization block of auditory/vestibular neurons → attack. Option B: LOW-frequency SNHL is earliest (not high frequency). Option C: Gadolinium-enhanced MRI can show hydrops but is not always positive and not routinely used for diagnosis — diagnosis is clinical (AAO-HNS criteria). Option D: Intratympanic gentamicin (chemical labyrinthectomy) controls vertigo but SACRIFICES hearing — used only when hearing is already severely impaired. Intratympanic steroids are hearing-preserving. PEARL: Glycerol test positive (>15 dB or >10% improvement) = confirms endolymphatic hydrops.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 50-year-old man presents with brief episodes (30–60 seconds) of severe vertigo triggered by rolling over in bed or looking up. Episodes have occurred for 3 weeks. Dix-Hallpike test on the right side produces upbeat-torsional nystagmus with latency of 3 seconds, fatigability, and duration <1 minute. The nystagmus fast phase beats toward the affected (right) ear. What is the MOST appropriate primary treatment?

options.A: Epley canalith repositioning maneuver for right posterior semicircular canal
options.B: Semont liberatory maneuver for right horizontal semicircular canal
options.C: Brandt-Daroff exercises as first-line treatment
options.D: Betahistine 16 mg TDS for 3 months

questions.explanation: Classic posterior BPPV (commonest, 80–90%): Dix-Hallpike → upbeat torsional nystagmus (fast phase toward affected ear when head turned to that side), latency 3–10 sec, fatigable, duration <1 min. Treatment = Epley canalith repositioning maneuver (CRM) — 80–90% single-session cure. Option B: Semont maneuver targets posterior canal BPPV too, but Epley is first-line; horizontal canal BPPV uses Lempert/BBQ roll. Option C: Brandt-Daroff is home-based habituation exercise for patients who cannot undergo CRM — second line. Option D: Betahistine is for Meniere's disease (not BPPV). PEARL: Horizontal canal BPPV → supine roll test → direction-changing nystagmus → BBQ roll (Lempert maneuver).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 40-year-old man presents with sudden right-sided complete facial nerve palsy (House-Brackmann Grade VI), preceded 2 days ago by severe right ear pain, vesicles in the right pinna and EAC, and sensorineural hearing loss with vertigo. Which of the following statements about this condition and its management is MOST correct?

options.A: It is caused by HSV-1 reactivation and is clinically identical to Bell's palsy
options.B: Oral acyclovir alone is the first-line treatment; steroids are contraindicated
options.C: Ramsay Hunt syndrome (VZV reactivation) with combined antiviral + steroid therapy gives better prognosis than Bell's palsy
options.D: Complete recovery occurs in >90% of cases similar to Bell's palsy outcomes

questions.explanation: Ramsay Hunt syndrome = VZV (HHV-3) reactivation in geniculate ganglion. Triad: facial nerve palsy + herpetic vesicles (pinna/EAC/palate) + SNHL/vertigo. Management: Antiviral (acyclovir/valacyclovir) + prednisolone (combined). Prognosis WORSE than Bell's palsy: only 50–70% complete recovery vs >85% in Bell's. Option A: HSV-1 causes Bell's palsy; VZV causes Ramsay Hunt — they are NOT identical (Ramsay Hunt has vesicles, cochlear/vestibular involvement, worse prognosis). Option B: Steroids are NOT contraindicated — combination antiviral + steroid is standard (superior to either alone). Option D: Complete recovery rate ~50–70%, significantly worse than Bell's palsy. PEARL: Grade VI (complete palsy) = House-Brackmann worst grade. EMG/ENoG guide surgery if indicated.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 6-year-old child is referred for evaluation of delayed speech and inattentiveness in class. Parents report recurrent ear infections. Tympanometry shows bilateral Type B tympanograms with absent stapedial reflexes. Pure tone audiometry (with play audiometry) shows bilateral 35 dB conductive hearing loss. What is the MOST appropriate management?

options.A: Hearing aids and speech therapy without surgical intervention
options.B: Bilateral myringotomy with grommet (ventilation tube) insertion
options.C: Adenotonsillectomy alone is curative
options.D: Watchful waiting for 3 more months with repeat audiometry

questions.explanation: Otitis media with effusion (OME/'glue ear'): bilateral Type B tympanogram + absent stapedial reflexes + conductive HL + speech delay. NICE/AAO-HNS guidelines: watchful waiting 3 months FIRST — but this child already has speech delay and 35 dB bilateral HL affecting development. Indication for VT insertion: bilateral HL >25 dB persisting >3 months WITH speech/developmental impact. Grommet = first-line surgical treatment. Option A: Hearing aids inappropriate as first line when surgical correction is possible/indicated. Option C: Adenoidectomy may be added (reduces recurrence), but grommet is the primary intervention for the effusion. Option D: Watchful waiting appropriate for mild cases without developmental impact — not here. PEARL: Type B = flat tympanogram = middle ear effusion. Type C = negative pressure (Eustachian tube dysfunction). Type A = normal.

questions.subject: ENT
key_findings: Intensely enhancing mass at right cerebellopontine angle (CPA)
Extension into internal auditory canal (IAC) — ice cream cone appearance
Widening of right IAC
Compression of adjacent brainstem
No calcification within mass
Left CPA normal
questions.question_text: A 48-year-old man presents with progressive unilateral right-sided SNHL, tinnitus, and subtle balance disturbance for 2 years. MRI with gadolinium (shown) reveals an enhancing CPA mass with IAC extension (ice cream cone appearance). ABR shows prolonged wave I–V interpeak latency on the right. Which of the following management decisions is MOST appropriate for a 2.5 cm intracanalicular/CPA tumour in this patient?

options.A: Watchful waiting with repeat MRI in 5 years is appropriate for any size
options.B: Stereotactic radiosurgery (Gamma Knife) is preferred for tumours >3 cm
options.C: Microsurgical excision via translabyrinthine/retrosigmoid approach is appropriate with counselling about hearing and facial nerve risks
options.D: Intratympanic steroids can shrink the tumour and restore hearing

questions.explanation: Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma, misnomer): arises from Schwann cells of superior vestibular nerve (CN VIII) in IAC. 2.5 cm tumour in a symptomatic patient = surgical candidate. Options: (1) Translabyrinthine approach — sacrifice hearing, good facial nerve exposure; (2) Retrosigmoid/suboccipital — hearing preservation possible; (3) Middle fossa — small intracanalicular, hearing preservation. Option A: Watchful waiting (MRI surveillance) is for small (<1.5 cm) or elderly patients — not a growing symptomatic 2.5 cm tumour. Option B: Gamma Knife is for small-medium tumours (<3 cm) not suitable for surgery, or elderly/high-risk — can be considered, but microsurgery is appropriate for this size/age. Option D: Intratympanic steroids have NO role in schwannoma treatment. PEARL: Bilateral acoustic neuromas = NF2 (neurofibromatosis type 2) — merlin protein mutation, chromosome 22.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 65-year-old hypertensive man presents to A&E with brisk right-sided posterior epistaxis. He is on warfarin (INR 3.8) for atrial fibrillation. Direct pressure for 20 minutes and anterior nasal packing have failed to control bleeding. On examination, BP is 160/100 mmHg; he is swallowing blood. What is the MOST appropriate next step?

options.A: IV vitamin K 10 mg and fresh frozen plasma, then posterior nasal packing
options.B: Posterior nasal pack (Brighton/Foley catheter) placement as immediate step
options.C: Emergency surgical ligation of the sphenopalatine artery
options.D: Endoscopic sphenopalatine artery cauterization after INR correction

questions.explanation: Posterior epistaxis with failed anterior packing and ongoing haemorrhage requires posterior nasal packing as the immediate next step (Foley catheter balloon/Brighton balloon). Simultaneously, INR reversal (vitamin K + FFP/PCC) should be initiated. Option A: Correct to reverse anticoagulation, but cannot wait — posterior pack FIRST to achieve haemostasis, INR reversal concurrently. Option C: Surgical ligation is reserved for failed packing. Option D: Endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation/cauterization (ESAL) is gold standard definitive treatment but performed electively after stabilization or when posterior packing fails. PEARL: Little's area (Kiesselbach's plexus, anterior septum) = anterior epistaxis. Posterior epistaxis source = sphenopalatine artery (branch of maxillary artery) — more severe, often requires posterior packing.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.image_title: Coronal CT Paranasal Sinuses (Soft Tissue Window)
key_findings: Complete opacification of right maxillary sinus
Bowing of medial maxillary sinus wall (lateral nasal wall)
Heterogeneous density within sinus (soft tissue + areas of calcification)
Expansion and thinning of sinus walls
Osteomeatal complex obstruction on right
No evidence of bony erosion
questions.question_text: A 30-year-old man presents with right-sided nasal obstruction, foul-smelling unilateral nasal discharge, and cheek fullness for 6 months. He has no fever. CT PNS (shown) reveals complete right maxillary sinus opacification with bowing of the medial wall, heterogeneous density with calcification, and no bony erosion. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?

options.A: Chronic maxillary rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps
options.B: Antrochoanal polyp
options.C: Maxillary sinus mucocele
options.D: Maxillary sinus fungal ball (aspergilloma)

questions.explanation: Maxillary sinus fungal ball (mycetoma/aspergilloma): Unilateral, foul smell, CT shows heterogeneous density with CALCIFICATION (hyperdense foci = calcium oxalate crystals from Aspergillus), bowing of walls, no bony erosion (non-invasive). Treatment = FESS (Caldwell-Luc/endoscopic washout). Option A: Chronic sinusitis with polyps = bilateral, homogeneous mucosal thickening, no calcification. Option B: Antrochoanal polyp = smooth soft tissue mass extending from antrum through choana into nasopharynx, NO calcification. Option C: Mucocele = homogeneous low-density mucoid fluid, expansion without calcification, occurs in frontal/ethmoid most commonly. PEARL: Calcification in sinus = think fungal ball. Bony erosion = invasive fungal sinusitis (medical emergency, especially in immunocompromised).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 35-year-old woman with known asthma presents with bilateral nasal obstruction, anosmia, and watery rhinorrhoea for 2 years. She also reports aspirin sensitivity (worsening asthma/urticaria after NSAIDs). Nasal endoscopy reveals multiple bilateral pale, glistening, grape-like masses arising from the middle meatus. What is this triad called, and what is the pathophysiology?

options.A: Kartagener syndrome — due to dynein arm defect causing impaired mucociliary clearance
options.B: Samter's triad — due to arachidonic acid pathway shunting from COX to 5-LOX causing excess leukotriene production
options.C: Young's syndrome — obstructive azoospermia with chronic sinopulmonary disease
options.D: Churg-Strauss syndrome — eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis causing nasal polyps

questions.explanation: Samter's triad (Aspirin-Exacerbated Respiratory Disease, AERD) = Nasal polyps + Asthma + Aspirin/NSAID sensitivity. Pathophysiology: COX-1 inhibition by aspirin → arachidonic acid shunted to 5-lipoxygenase pathway → excess cysteinyl leukotrienes (LTC4, LTD4, LTE4) → bronchoconstriction, mucosal oedema, polyp formation. Option A: Kartagener = situs inversus + bronchiectasis + sinusitis (dynein defect). Option C: Young's syndrome = sinusitis + bronchiectasis + obstructive azoospermia (inspissated secretions). Option D: Churg-Strauss (EGPA) can have polyps but the triad described is Samter's. PEARL: Management: intranasal steroids, aspirin desensitization, leukotriene antagonists (montelukast), endoscopic sinus surgery for refractory cases. Biologics (dupilumab) for severe refractory CRS with polyps.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 25-year-old man presents with unilateral nasal obstruction and recurrent headaches. Anterior rhinoscopy shows a C-shaped septal deviation to the right with a compensatory hypertrophy of the left inferior turbinate. He has failed medical management. What is the surgical procedure of choice, and at what age is it safe to perform?

options.A: Rhinoplasty — can be done at any age after 16 years
options.B: Submucous resection (SMR) — can be done at any age after puberty (17–18 years in females, 18 years in males)
options.C: Septoplasty (Killian's operation) — preferred after completion of nasal growth (17–18 years), can be done earlier if symptoms severe
options.D: Functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS) — first-line for septal deviation

questions.explanation: Septoplasty (conservative, mucosal-sparing technique) is preferred over SMR (which removes cartilage, risks saddle nose deformity). Nasal septal growth is complete by 17–18 years, so surgery is preferably deferred until then to avoid disrupting growth centres. Option A: Rhinoplasty = cosmetic reshaping of the external nose — not for functional septal deviation. Option B: SMR (Killian's operation historically) resects cartilaginous septum — risk of saddle nose, perforation; septoplasty has replaced it as the gold standard. Option D: FESS is for sinusitis/polyps, not primary septal deviation. PEARL: Compensatory turbinate hypertrophy on the opposite side of deviation = due to chronic reduced airflow causing paradoxical turbinate enlargement.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 20-year-old medical student presents with perennial sneezing (>4 episodes/morning), watery rhinorrhoea, nasal itching, and bilateral nasal obstruction. Symptoms are present throughout the year and worsen at home. Skin prick test shows a 7 mm wheal to house dust mite. Nasal smear shows >10% eosinophils. He has tried loratadine with partial relief. According to ARIA guidelines, what is the NEXT BEST treatment step?

options.A: Add montelukast (leukotriene receptor antagonist) and continue loratadine
options.B: Switch to second-generation antihistamine with intranasal corticosteroid (INCS)
options.C: Start allergen immunotherapy (AIT) immediately as first-line
options.D: Prescribe oral prednisolone 30 mg for 2 weeks to control inflammation

questions.explanation: ARIA (Allergic Rhinitis and its Impact on Asthma) guidelines: Moderate-severe persistent allergic rhinitis uncontrolled on antihistamine alone → ADD intranasal corticosteroid (INCS). INCS is the most effective single drug class for allergic rhinitis (reduces all symptoms including obstruction, which antihistamines poorly address). Loratadine alone (antihistamine) + INCS = step-up. Option A: Montelukast has modest benefit — INCS is superior. Option C: AIT is indicated for moderate-severe allergic rhinitis inadequately controlled on pharmacotherapy — not the immediate next step at this stage. Option D: Oral steroids are not recommended for routine allergic rhinitis management due to systemic side effects. PEARL: INCS > oral antihistamines for nasal obstruction. Fluticasone, mometasone have minimal systemic bioavailability (<1%).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 55-year-old male woodworker presents with unilateral nasal obstruction, bloody nasal discharge, and right-sided facial pain for 6 months. CT shows a soft tissue mass in the right nasal cavity and ethmoid sinuses with bony destruction. Biopsy shows a transitional-type epithelial neoplasm with papillary architecture, cellular atypia, and an inverted growth pattern. What is the MOST likely diagnosis, and what is the risk that makes surveillance mandatory?

options.A: Squamous cell carcinoma of the nasal cavity — risk of nodal metastasis
options.B: Adenocarcinoma of ethmoid sinus (woodworker's cancer) — risk of intracranial extension
options.C: Inverted papilloma (Schneiderian papilloma) — risk of synchronous or metachronous malignant transformation (10–15%)
options.D: Olfactory neuroblastoma (esthesioneuroblastoma) — risk of CSF rhinorrhoea

questions.explanation: Inverted papilloma: Lateral nasal wall (middle meatus) origin, inverted growth into stroma on histology, locally aggressive, destroys bone, HIGH RECURRENCE after excision, 10–15% risk of squamous cell carcinoma transformation (synchronous or metachronous). Treatment: Endoscopic or open medial maxillectomy with wide margins + lifelong surveillance endoscopy. Option B: Adenocarcinoma of ethmoid sinus IS a woodworker/leather worker cancer (hardwood dust exposure) — but biopsy here shows inverted papilloma histology. Option D: Olfactory neuroblastoma = Hyams grading, olfactory epithelium origin, S100/synaptophysin+. Option A: SCC would show invasive squamous cells without inverted architecture. PEARL: Woodworker + sinonasal adenocarcinoma = occupational cancer. Inverted papilloma + SCC transformation = the critical risk for surveillance.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 16-year-old presents with recurrent sore throat, fever, and difficulty swallowing occurring 5 times in the past year and 4 times the year before. Each episode was confirmed as acute tonsillitis requiring antibiotics. Parents ask about tonsillectomy. According to Paradise criteria, is this patient eligible?

options.A: No — requires 7 or more episodes per year
options.B: Yes — Paradise criteria require ≥7 per year for 1 year, OR ≥5 per year for 2 years, OR ≥3 per year for 3 years
options.C: No — tonsillectomy is only indicated for airway obstruction, not recurrent infections
options.D: Yes — any patient with >3 episodes in a year qualifies for tonsillectomy

questions.explanation: Paradise criteria for tonsillectomy (recurrent acute tonsillitis): ≥7 episodes/year for 1 year, OR ≥5 episodes/year for 2 consecutive years, OR ≥3 episodes/year for 3 consecutive years — each episode must be documented with: temperature >38.3°C, cervical lymphadenopathy, tonsillar exudate, or positive streptococcal culture. This patient has 5 episodes (year 1) + 4 episodes (year 2) = meets the '≥5 per year for 2 years' criterion. Option A: 7/year is the 1-year threshold, not the only criterion. Option C: Airway obstruction (OSA) is also an indication, but recurrent infection qualifies under Paradise criteria. Option D: 3/year alone requires 3 consecutive years. PEARL: Also indicated for peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) — second ipsilateral quinsy is absolute indication.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 22-year-old man presents with severe sore throat, trismus, muffled ('hot potato') voice, drooling, and uvular deviation to the LEFT. On examination, there is a bulge in the right peritonsillar area with medial displacement of the right tonsil. He has been on amoxicillin for 5 days for tonsillitis. What is the MOST appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Increase amoxicillin dose and add metronidazole; admit for IV antibiotics
options.B: CT neck to confirm abscess before any intervention
options.C: Needle aspiration or incision and drainage of the peritonsillar abscess plus IV antibiotics
options.D: Emergency tonsillectomy under general anaesthesia

questions.explanation: Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy): Collection above superior pole of tonsil between capsule and superior constrictor. Classic features: trismus, muffled voice, uvular deviation to OPPOSITE side (contralateral — pus pushes uvula away), drooling. Management: Needle aspiration (office procedure, diagnostic + therapeutic) or I&D + IV benzylpenicillin + metronidazole (mixed aerobe/anaerobe flora). Option A: Failed oral amoxicillin for 5 days = antibiotic failure, abscess formed — antibiotics alone insufficient once pus has collected. Option B: Clinical diagnosis sufficient; CT adds delay (reserved for deep space spread). Option D: Hot/Interval tonsillectomy — interval tonsillectomy 6 weeks later for recurrent quinsy; emergency ('quinsy tonsillectomy') if aspiration fails or airway compromised. PEARL: Common organisms: Group A Strep + Fusobacterium necrophorum + oral anaerobes.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 4-year-old unimmunized child presents to the emergency department with high fever (39.5°C), drooling, dysphagia, inspiratory stridor, and sitting in a 'tripod position' (leaning forward, hands on knees). The child appears toxic and anxious. Parents report rapid onset over 4 hours. What is the SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT next step?

options.A: Lateral neck X-ray to confirm 'thumbprint sign' before any intervention
options.B: Direct laryngoscopy in the emergency bay to visualize the epiglottis
options.C: Secure the airway in a controlled setting (operating theatre) by experienced personnel; avoid distressing the child
options.D: IV ceftriaxone and high-flow oxygen; reassess in 30 minutes

questions.explanation: Acute epiglottitis (Haemophilus influenzae type B, now rare post-Hib vaccine — seen in unimmunized): Medical EMERGENCY. Tripod position, drooling, muffled voice, rapid onset = hallmarks. DO NOT: examine throat in A&E, take to X-ray, upset the child — any agitation may precipitate complete airway obstruction and cardiorespiratory arrest. Secure airway FIRST in OT under GA by ENT + anaesthetics team (intubation/tracheostomy on standby). THEN antibiotics (IV cefotaxime/ceftriaxone). Option A: X-ray appropriate ONLY if diagnosis uncertain and child stable — NOT here; delays airway management. Option B: Direct laryngoscopy in uncontrolled environment may precipitate complete obstruction. Option D: Antibiotics are second priority; airway is first. PEARL: Lateral neck X-ray = 'thumbprint sign' = thickened epiglottis. Vallecula sign (loss of vallecula air space) also seen. Croup = 'steeple sign' on AP neck X-ray.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 60-year-old male chronic smoker and alcoholic presents with progressive dysphagia to solids first then liquids, weight loss of 8 kg in 3 months, and a right neck mass for 4 months. Hoarseness developed recently. Flexible nasolaryngoscopy shows a large pyriform fossa mass with fixation of the right vocal cord. Biopsy confirms SCC. Staging CT shows the primary tumor, right level II-IV lymph nodes (largest 3.5 cm), no distant metastasis. What is his TNM staging?

options.A: T2 N2 M0 — Stage III
options.B: T3 N2b M0 — Stage IVA
options.C: T4a N2b M0 — Stage IVA
options.D: T3 N1 M0 — Stage III

questions.explanation: Hypopharyngeal SCC (pyriform fossa, commonest site ~70%): T staging: T3 = invasion of adjacent structures OR fixation of hemilarynx (vocal cord fixation = T3). T4a = invasion of thyroid/cricoid cartilage, hyoid, thyroid gland, oesophagus, or central compartment soft tissue. N staging: N2b = multiple ipsilateral nodes, none >6 cm. Multiple right neck nodes = N2b. M0 = no distant mets. Vocal cord fixation → T3. Multiple ipsilateral nodes (II, III, IV) ≤6 cm = N2b. T3N2bM0 = Stage IVA. Option A: T2 = limited to one subsite of hypopharynx; cord fixation escalates to T3. Option C: T4a requires cartilage/thyroid/oesophagus invasion — not stated. Option D: N1 = single ipsilateral node ≤3 cm; multiple nodes here = N2b. PEARL: Hypopharyngeal SCC has worst prognosis of all head/neck SCC — presents late, high nodal spread, distant mets in 20–30%.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 35-year-old female primary school teacher presents with progressive hoarseness, voice fatigue, and loss of high-pitched notes for 8 months. She uses her voice extensively and is a social smoker. Videolaryngoscopy shows bilateral symmetrical swellings at the junction of the anterior one-third and posterior two-thirds of the vocal cords. The swellings are pale, sessile, and firm. Voice rest partially improves symptoms. What is the diagnosis and BEST initial management?

options.A: Vocal cord polyp — microlaryngoscopic excision as first line
options.B: Vocal cord nodules — voice therapy (vocal hygiene and voice rehabilitation) as first line
options.C: Reinke's oedema — smoking cessation and voice therapy; surgery if failed
options.D: Vocal cord cyst — microlaryngoscopic deroofing as first line

questions.explanation: Vocal cord nodules ('singer's nodules', 'teacher's nodules'): bilateral, symmetrical, at the junction of anterior 1/3 and posterior 2/3 (maximum vibration point). Pale, firm, sessile. Caused by vocal abuse. FIRST-LINE = voice therapy (address vocal habits, reduce strain, vocal hygiene). Surgery only for nodules not responding after 6–12 months of therapy. Option A: Vocal cord polyp = unilateral, usually pedunculated/sessile, haemorrhagic — primary treatment is microlaryngoscopic excision. Option C: Reinke's oedema = diffuse bilateral gelatinous swelling (entire cord), associated with smoking and hypothyroidism — voice therapy + smoking cessation; surgery (decortication) if needed. Option D: Vocal cord cyst = subepithelial, unilateral — surgery needed. PEARL: Bilateral symmetrical junction-1/3 junction lesion in voice professional = nodules → voice therapy FIRST.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 58-year-old male smoker presents with 4-month history of hoarseness. Flexible laryngoscopy shows a leukoplakic lesion confined to the left true vocal cord with normal cord mobility. Biopsy shows moderate dysplasia (CIN II/VAIN II equivalent). CT and MRI show no extension beyond the cord and no nodal disease. What is the MOST appropriate management and what is the staging?

options.A: T1a N0 M0 — total laryngectomy is the treatment of choice
options.B: T1a N0 M0 — radiotherapy alone is the standard of care for T1 glottic lesions
options.C: T1a N0 M0 — microlaryngoscopic laser excision (CO2 laser cordectomy) or radiotherapy are both acceptable with equivalent cure rates
options.D: T2 N0 M0 — the lesion involves the entire cord so extended resection is needed

questions.explanation: T1a glottic carcinoma: confined to one vocal cord, normal mobility. Both CO2 laser cordectomy (transoral microlaryngoscopy) and radiotherapy offer 85–95% local control rates, with equivalent overall survival. Laser surgery: immediate, single session, preserves cartilage framework, but may require repeat for margins. Radiotherapy: better voice quality outcomes in some studies, 6 weeks treatment. Patient preference/centre expertise guides choice. Option A: Total laryngectomy is radical and reserved for T4/recurrence after definitive treatment — NOT for T1a. Option B: Radiotherapy alone is NOT the only standard — laser excision is equally valid and often preferred at high-volume centres. Option D: T1a is confined to ONE cord with normal mobility — T2 would be impaired mobility or extension to supraglottis/subglottis. PEARL: Glottic SCC presents EARLY with hoarseness (good prognosis). Supraglottic SCC presents late with nodal mets (rich lymphatics, poor prognosis at presentation).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 45-year-old non-smoker man presents with a 3 × 4 cm right upper neck mass for 3 months. He has no pharyngeal symptoms, no weight loss, and no primary visible lesion on oral examination. Fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) of the neck mass shows non-keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma. PET-CT shows the neck mass FDG-avid; no identifiable primary. Bilateral tonsillectomy is performed and the right tonsil shows occult SCC. What is the MOST LIKELY aetiological agent for this presentation?

options.A: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)
options.B: Human papillomavirus (HPV), predominantly HPV-16
options.C: Tobacco and alcohol synergism
options.D: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8)

questions.explanation: HPV-associated oropharyngeal SCC (OPSCC): HPV-16 (>90% of HPV+ OPSCC). Classic profile: non-smoker, younger male, cystic neck node (from tonsillar/BOT primary), non-keratinizing SCC on histology, p16 immunostaining positive. Unknown primary neck SCC in this demographic = HPV-associated oropharyngeal SCC until proven otherwise. Tonsil/base of tongue biopsy/tonsillectomy reveals occult primary. BETTER prognosis than HPV-negative OPSCC. Option A: EBV = nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC), Southeast Asian/Chinese patients, undifferentiated non-keratinizing carcinoma of nasopharynx, not tonsillar. Option C: Tobacco/alcohol = conventional head and neck SCC, keratinizing, older patients, multiple subsites. Option D: HHV-8 = Kaposi sarcoma. PEARL: p16 overexpression (surrogate marker for HPV) = better prognosis, responds better to treatment, de-escalation protocols under study.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 32-year-old woman presents with a 2 cm right thyroid nodule discovered incidentally. She has no compressive symptoms. Ultrasound shows a solid hypoechoic nodule with microcalcifications, irregular margins, and increased intranodular vascularity — TIRADS 5. FNAC (Bethesda System) shows Bethesda Category V (suspicious for malignancy). What is the MOST appropriate next step?

options.A: Repeat FNAC in 6 months as a single suspicious sample may be false positive
options.B: Total thyroidectomy with central neck dissection
options.C: Right hemithyroidectomy (lobectomy) as diagnostic and potentially therapeutic procedure
options.D: Radioactive iodine ablation before surgery to reduce tumour size

questions.explanation: Bethesda V (Suspicious for Malignancy): risk of malignancy 60–75%. ATA and NCCN guidelines: For a 1–4 cm nodule classified Bethesda V, right hemithyroidectomy/lobectomy is appropriate — it is both diagnostic (final histology) and potentially therapeutic (if PTC confined to one lobe, lobectomy may be curative for low-risk disease). Total thyroidectomy is preferred if: bilateral disease, high-risk features (>4 cm, extrathyroidal extension, clinical lymphadenopathy). Option A: TIRADS 5 + Bethesda V = high malignancy risk — repeat FNAC is not appropriate; surgery indicated. Option B: Total thyroidectomy ± central neck dissection is appropriate if final histology confirms high-risk PTC or bilateral disease — but hemithyroidectomy first is a reasonable initial approach for this isolated nodule. Option D: RAI ablation is postoperative for differentiated thyroid cancer — NEVER preoperative. PEARL: Bethesda I=non-diagnostic, II=benign, III=AUS, IV=FN, V=suspicious, VI=malignant.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 55-year-old man presents with a slowly growing right parotid mass for 2 years. It is painless, 3 cm, mobile, soft to firm, and located at the lower pole of the right parotid. FNAC shows both epithelial and mesenchymal (stromal) components — a biphasic pattern with chondromyxoid stroma. What is the diagnosis and treatment?

options.A: Warthin's tumour (papillary cystadenoma lymphomatosum) — superficial parotidectomy
options.B: Pleomorphic adenoma (mixed salivary tumour) — superficial parotidectomy with adequate margins
options.C: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma — total parotidectomy with facial nerve sacrifice
options.D: Basal cell adenoma — enucleation is curative

questions.explanation: Pleomorphic adenoma: Commonest salivary gland tumour (60–70%), commonest in parotid (80%), lower pole, painless, slow-growing, biphasic histology (epithelial + myoepithelial cells + chondromyxoid stroma = pleomorphic/mixed pattern). Treatment: Superficial parotidectomy (not enucleation — high recurrence with enucleation due to pseudopod extensions). Facial nerve preserved. Risk of malignant transformation (carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma) = 5–10% in long-standing untreated lesions. Option A: Warthin's tumour = bilateral, tail of parotid, elderly males, smokers, lymphoid stroma with oncocytic epithelium — surgical excision/superficial parotidectomy. Option C: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma = commonest malignant parotid tumour; facial nerve involvement = malignancy sign. Option D: Enucleation of pleomorphic adenoma = high recurrence (not recommended). PEARL: ALL parotid tumours — facial nerve mapping is essential preoperatively.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 25-year-old woman presents with a painless fluctuant swelling along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle at the junction of upper and middle thirds. It has been present since childhood and occasionally discharges mucoid fluid. It transilluminates. What is the MOST likely diagnosis and the embryological origin?

options.A: Thyroglossal cyst — remnant of thyroglossal duct from foramen caecum
options.B: Branchial (cleft) cyst — remnant of second branchial arch/cleft/pouch complex
options.C: Cystic hygroma — lymphatic malformation of posterior triangle
options.D: Dermoid cyst — ectodermal remnant along fusion lines

questions.explanation: Second branchial cleft cyst (commonest type, ~95% of branchial anomalies): Location = along anterior border of SCM at junction of upper and middle thirds. Fluid = cholesterol-rich fluid with lymphoid tissue lining. Origin: failed obliteration of cervical sinus (of His) formed by second arch overgrowth. Internal opening (if sinus present) = tonsillar fossa. Option A: Thyroglossal cyst = midline, moves on swallowing and tongue protrusion, anywhere from foramen caecum to isthmus of thyroid. Option C: Cystic hygroma = posterior triangle, presents in infancy/childhood, multilocular, soft, brilliantly transilluminates — different location and age. Option D: Dermoid cyst = midline face/neck/floor of mouth, doughy, doesn't transilluminate. PEARL: Treatment of branchial cyst = complete surgical excision of cyst ± tract to prevent recurrence. Recurrence after incomplete excision = common pitfall.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 68-year-old diabetic (poorly controlled, HbA1c 11%) presents with severe unremitting right ear pain, greenish discharge, granulation tissue at the bony-cartilaginous junction of the right EAC, and now has right-sided facial nerve palsy. ESR is 110 mm/hr. CT temporal bone shows soft tissue in the right EAC with adjacent bony erosion. Tc-99m bone scan shows increased uptake. What is the diagnosis and MOST appropriate management?

options.A: Acute otitis externa — oral ciprofloxacin drops for 2 weeks
options.B: Malignant (necrotising) otitis externa — prolonged IV/oral antipseudomonal therapy (ciprofloxacin) for 6–8 weeks with surgical debridement
options.C: Cholesteatoma with facial nerve involvement — cortical mastoidectomy
options.D: Invasive fungal otitis — amphotericin B IV for 8 weeks

questions.explanation: Malignant (Necrotising) Otitis Externa (MOE): Elderly diabetics or immunocompromised. Causative organism: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (>95%). Hallmarks: severe pain disproportionate to exam, granulation tissue at bony-cartilaginous junction, spreading to skull base → cranial nerve palsies (VII first, then IX, X, XI, XII). Investigations: ESR elevated (activity marker), Tc-99m bone scan (early osteomyelitis), CT shows bony erosion. Treatment: Prolonged anti-pseudomonal ciprofloxacin (oral or IV, 6–12 weeks) + glycaemic control + surgical debridement of necrotic tissue + hyperbaric oxygen (adjunct). Option A: Simple otitis externa has no bone involvement, no cranial nerve palsy. Option C: Cholesteatoma has different history/otoscopy findings. Option D: Fungal MOE (Aspergillus) can occur but Pseudomonas is by far most common. PEARL: ESR is the best marker to monitor treatment response in MOE (should decrease with treatment).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.image_title: Otoscopic View of Right Tympanic Membrane
key_findings: Pearly grey translucent membrane
Cone of light (light reflex) at 5 o'clock position (right ear)
Pars tensa visible — intact
Malleus handle and lateral process visible
Pars flaccida (Shrapnell's membrane) at superior portion
Annulus intact around periphery
questions.question_text: Regarding the normal tympanic membrane (otoscopic view shown), which of the following statements is INCORRECT?

options.A: The cone of light is seen antero-inferiorly and is at 5 o'clock in the right ear
options.B: The pars flaccida (Shrapnell's membrane) is supero-anteriorly located, above the lateral process of the malleus
options.C: The attic cholesteatoma typically begins with a retraction pocket in the pars flaccida region
options.D: The tympanic membrane is innervated entirely by the auriculotemporal branch of the mandibular nerve (CN V3)

questions.explanation: The tympanic membrane has MULTIPLE nerve supplies — NOT solely auriculotemporal nerve (V3). Innervation: Outer surface: auriculotemporal (V3) anteriorly, Arnold's nerve (auricular branch of vagus X) posteriorly. Inner surface: glossopharyngeal (IX) (Jacobson's nerve). This multi-nerve supply explains referred otalgia: cardiac pain (vagus), tongue base cancer (IX), dental pain (V3), laryngeal cancer (X) can all refer to the ear. Option A: Correct — cone of light antero-inferiorly, 5 o'clock right, 7 o'clock left. Option B: Correct — Shrapnell's membrane = pars flaccida, lacks fibrous middle layer, supero-anterior, above lateral process of malleus. Option C: Correct — attic retraction starts at pars flaccida → epitympanic cholesteatoma. PEARL: Referred otalgia = pain from distant site perceived in ear due to shared innervation — always examine tongue base, tonsil, larynx, teeth.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 30-year-old man presents with clear watery nasal discharge from the right nostril that increases when he bends forward. He had a road traffic accident 6 weeks ago involving head injury. The discharge forms a 'halo/ring sign' on filter paper. Beta-2 transferrin test on the nasal fluid is positive. MRI cisternography localizes the leak to the cribriform plate region. What is the MOST appropriate management?

options.A: Lumbar drain insertion and bed rest for 2 weeks as first-line
options.B: Endoscopic skull base repair (endoscopic CSF leak repair) with fat/fascia graft
options.C: Open craniotomy with dural repair as first-line for post-traumatic CSF leak
options.D: Conservative management only — 90% of traumatic CSF leaks close spontaneously

questions.explanation: Post-traumatic CSF rhinorrhoea: most resolve spontaneously within 1 week. After 6 weeks of persistent leak, surgical repair is indicated (spontaneous closure unlikely). Endoscopic skull base repair = gold standard for anterior skull base CSF leaks (cribriform plate, fovea ethmoidalis). Technique: Free flap (fat, fascia lata, turbinate mucosal flap) + fibrin glue. >90% success rate. Option A: Lumbar drain (CSF diversion) is used as primary treatment for low-flow leaks or as an adjunct post-surgery — NOT standard first-line after 6 weeks of failed conservative management. Option C: Open craniotomy is reserved for failed endoscopic repair or complex lateral skull base/posterior fossa leaks. Option D: Spontaneous closure occurs in ~85% within 7 days of injury — after 6 weeks, unlikely; also risk of meningitis with persistent leak. PEARL: Beta-2 transferrin = gold standard biochemical marker for CSF (unique to CSF/perilymph). Halo/ring sign = screening test only.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 38-year-old woman presents with bilateral nasal obstruction, recurrent epistaxis, saddle nose deformity, and oral ulcers. She also has haemoptysis and haematuria. CXR shows bilateral cavitating nodules. ANCA testing shows c-ANCA positive (anti-PR3). Renal biopsy shows necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis with pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis. What is the MOST appropriate induction treatment?

options.A: Oral prednisolone alone as first-line for limited disease
options.B: Rituximab or cyclophosphamide combined with high-dose glucocorticoids
options.C: Methotrexate maintenance therapy immediately without induction
options.D: Plasmapheresis as first-line to remove ANCA antibodies

questions.explanation: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA, formerly Wegener's): c-ANCA (anti-PR3) positive, upper respiratory tract (saddle nose, nasal ulcers) + lower respiratory tract (cavitating nodules, haemoptysis) + renal involvement (pauci-immune crescentic GN) = classic triad. Severe/generalised disease (renal involvement): Induction = rituximab (preferred, non-inferior to cyclophosphamide, less toxic) OR IV cyclophosphamide PLUS high-dose IV methylprednisolone then oral prednisolone. Maintenance = rituximab or azathioprine + low-dose steroids. Option A: Steroids alone = inadequate for severe disease with renal involvement. Option C: Methotrexate is maintenance therapy for remission, not induction for severe disease. Option D: Plasmapheresis (plasma exchange) was previously used for severe renal disease — PEXIVAS trial showed no benefit; no longer routine. PEARL: Limited GPA (no life-threatening organ involvement) = methotrexate + prednisolone for induction.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 45-year-old obese man (BMI 34) presents with excessive daytime sleepiness (Epworth score 17/24), loud snoring, witnessed apnoeas, morning headaches, and nocturia. Overnight polysomnography shows apnoea-hypopnoea index (AHI) of 42/hour, oxygen desaturation to 78%, and predominantly obstructive events. What is the FIRST-LINE and MOST effective treatment for this severity?

options.A: Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty (UPPP) as first-line surgical management
options.B: Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) therapy
options.C: Mandibular advancement device (MAD) as equivalent first-line option for severe OSA
options.D: Weight loss counselling alone — adequate if BMI reduces to <30

questions.explanation: Severe OSA (AHI ≥30/hr): FIRST-LINE treatment = CPAP (Continuous Positive Airway Pressure). CPAP splints the airway open with positive pressure, abolishing obstructive apnoeas. Most effective treatment for all severities; improves AHI, daytime sleepiness, cardiovascular risk, cognitive function. Option A: UPPP (surgical soft palate/uvula reduction) is second-line for patients intolerant of CPAP; success rate ~50% for OSA; less effective than CPAP for severe disease. Option C: MAD is first-line for mild-moderate OSA OR CPAP-intolerant patients — not primary for severe OSA (AHI 42). Option D: Weight loss is adjunctive and important but insufficient as sole treatment for severe OSA with significant desaturation and cardiovascular risk. PEARL: AHI: Mild 5–14, Moderate 15–29, Severe ≥30. Berlin Questionnaire/STOP-BANG = screening tools. Epworth Sleepiness Scale ≥11 = excessive daytime sleepiness.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 3-day-old neonate fails newborn hearing screening bilaterally (TEOAE absent bilaterally). Parents report no family history of deafness. The child is otherwise well. Which of the following investigations is the NEXT step to confirm the hearing loss?

options.A: Pure tone audiometry — can be performed from birth
options.B: Auditory Brainstem Response (ABR/BERA) — objective test, can be performed in neonates
options.C: Tympanometry only to rule out middle ear effusion
options.D: Observation until 6 months and repeat TEOAE

questions.explanation: Newborn hearing screening: TEOAE (Transient Evoked OtoAcoustic Emissions) fail = refer for diagnostic ABR (Auditory Brainstem Response). ABR is the gold standard diagnostic test in neonates — objective, does not require patient cooperation, can differentiate sensorineural from conductive loss, identifies level of dysfunction. Option A: Pure tone audiometry requires active patient cooperation — not feasible in neonates; used from ~4 years (or play audiometry from 2.5 years). Option C: Tympanometry alone cannot diagnose SNHL and doesn't replace ABR. Option D: Delaying to 6 months is inappropriate — early identification and intervention (by 6 months of age) is critical for speech/language development (universal newborn hearing screening guidelines). PEARL: TEOAE tests outer hair cell (cochlear) function. ABR tests cochlear nerve and brainstem auditory pathway. AABR (automated ABR) = second-line screening; diagnostic ABR = definitive test.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 72-year-old retired teacher presents with bilateral gradually progressive hearing loss over 10 years. He complains of difficulty understanding speech, especially in background noise, and his family reports he turns up the TV volume excessively. Audiogram shows bilateral symmetrical high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss sloping from high to low frequencies. What is the MOST appropriate management?

options.A: Cochlear implant as first-line treatment for all cases of presbycusis
options.B: Hearing aids (digital, behind-the-ear or receiver-in-canal) and auditory rehabilitation
options.C: Vitamins and antioxidants to reverse cochlear degeneration
options.D: Reassurance — this is a normal ageing process requiring no treatment

questions.explanation: Presbycusis (age-related hearing loss): Bilateral symmetrical SNHL, high-frequency predominantly, gradual onset over decades. Caused by loss of hair cells (sensory type), strial degeneration (metabolic type), neuronal loss, or cochlear conductive changes. Management: Hearing aids (digital amplification with frequency shaping) are first-line — significantly improve communication and quality of life. Auditory rehabilitation (listening strategies, lip-reading) adjunctive. Option A: Cochlear implants reserved for severe-profound hearing loss (>70 dB HL) not adequately benefited by hearing aids. Option C: No evidence that vitamins/antioxidants reverse established presbycusis. Option D: Untreated presbycusis leads to social isolation, depression, and cognitive decline — active treatment is recommended. PEARL: WHO: >25 dB hearing loss = clinically significant. Presbycusis is the leading cause of hearing loss in adults worldwide.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 2-year-old child is brought with sudden onset choking, cyanosis, and respiratory distress while playing. Parents report the child may have swallowed a small toy. After initial choking episode, the child now has unilateral wheeze on chest auscultation and mild respiratory distress at rest. CXR shows air trapping (hyperinflation) of the right lung. What is the MOST appropriate management?

options.A: Emergency Heimlich maneuver and vigorous back blows to dislodge the foreign body
options.B: Urgent rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia for foreign body retrieval
options.C: High-flow oxygen and observation; repeat CXR in 4 hours
options.D: Flexible bronchoscopy as first-line for suspected bronchial foreign body in children

questions.explanation: Bronchial foreign body (right main bronchus more common — more vertical, larger diameter): After acute choking episode, the child has stabilized but has persistent wheeze, hyperinflation = ball-valve obstruction (air enters on inspiration, trapped on expiration). RIGID bronchoscopy under GA is the gold standard for foreign body retrieval in children — allows controlled airway, better visualization, and use of foreign body forceps. Option A: Heimlich/back blows = for complete acute airway obstruction with cyanosis/unconsciousness — NOT for a stable child with partial obstruction (could dislodge FB to cause complete obstruction). Option C: Observation unacceptable — risk of complete obstruction, infection, lung damage. Option D: Flexible bronchoscopy is diagnostic but lacks therapeutic capability for solid FB retrieval in children — rigid is preferred. PEARL: Expiratory CXR (or lateral decubitus) shows air trapping better. Peanuts/organic FB = most common; cause intense inflammation (don't delay removal).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 20-year-old man is slapped on the right ear and presents with immediate right-sided hearing loss and tinnitus. Otoscopy shows a small triangular perforation in the antero-inferior quadrant of the right tympanic membrane. There is no vertigo or facial nerve palsy. What is the MOST appropriate management?

options.A: Immediate surgical closure with fat or paper patch
options.B: Topical antibiotic ear drops to prevent secondary infection
options.C: Conservative management — keep ear dry, avoid nose blowing; majority heal spontaneously
options.D: Immediate referral for cochlear implant assessment

questions.explanation: Traumatic tympanic membrane perforation (blow/slap/blast): >80–90% of small perforations heal spontaneously within 3 months. Management: Keep dry (no water entry), avoid nose blowing (Valsalva-prevents displacement), no ear drops (potentially ototoxic cochlea if round window disrupted), review in 4–6 weeks. Option A: Surgery (myringoplasty/tympanoplasty) is reserved for perforations not healed after 3 months. Option B: Topical antibiotic drops are NOT recommended for fresh traumatic perforations — risk of ototoxicity (aminoglycoside drops through perforated drum) and can impair spontaneous healing. Option D: Cochlear implant is for profound SNHL, not indicated here. PEARL: Red flags requiring urgent ENT review: vertigo + hearing loss (possible perilymph fistula/ossicular disruption), facial nerve palsy, suspected middle ear involvement. Dry traumatic perforation in healthy TM = observe for spontaneous healing.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 40-year-old Chinese man presents with a 3-month history of painless right neck mass, right-sided conductive hearing loss (with right middle ear effusion), nasal obstruction, and epistaxis. EBV VCA IgA titre is markedly elevated. MRI shows a nasopharyngeal mass with extension to the parapharyngeal space and bilateral retropharyngeal lymphadenopathy. Biopsy shows undifferentiated non-keratinizing carcinoma. What is the TREATMENT OF CHOICE for this stage?

options.A: Surgical resection of the nasopharyngeal primary with neck dissection
options.B: Concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CCRT) with cisplatin
options.C: Radiotherapy alone to the nasopharynx and bilateral neck
options.D: Induction chemotherapy followed by radiotherapy without concurrent chemotherapy

questions.explanation: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC): EBV-associated (especially WHO type II/III undifferentiated), Southeast Asian predominance. Anatomically unresectable (nasopharynx close to skull base) — surgery is NOT primary treatment for NPC. Stage III/IVA (locally advanced, bilateral nodes): Standard of care = CONCURRENT CHEMORADIOTHERAPY (CCRT) with cisplatin as radiosensitizer + intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT). Induction + CCRT increasingly used for very advanced disease. Option A: Surgery is not primary treatment — NPC is highly radiosensitive. Neck dissection used for residual neck nodes post-RT. Option C: RT alone is reserved for Stage I (T1N0) disease only. Option D: Induction chemotherapy THEN concurrent CRT has emerging evidence but is NOT current standard for this stage — CCRT remains standard. PEARL: NPC triad: EBV + Chinese ethnicity + undifferentiated histology. Serous OME in adult Asian = rule out NPC. Fossa of Rosenmüller (lateral pharyngeal recess) = commonest site of origin.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 55-year-old woman presents with progressive dysphagia, hoarseness, and a neck mass that pulsates. She is an iron-deficiency anaemic, with koilonychia and glossitis. Endoscopy shows a postcricoid web. Biopsy of the web shows squamous metaplasia, no malignancy. What is this syndrome, and what is the most important concern in this condition?

options.A: Zenker's diverticulum — risk of aspiration pneumonia
options.B: Plummer-Vinson syndrome (Patterson-Kelly-Brown syndrome) — risk of postcricoid carcinoma
options.C: Achalasia — risk of aspiration and oesophageal carcinoma
options.D: Globus pharyngeus — psychosomatic condition with no malignant potential

questions.explanation: Plummer-Vinson syndrome (Patterson-Kelly-Brown / Paterson-Kelly syndrome): Triad = Iron deficiency anaemia + dysphagia (postcricoid web) + glossitis/koilonychia. Predominantly affects middle-aged women. Postcricoid web = anterior mucosal fold causing dysphagia to solids. CRITICAL risk = HIGH malignant potential for POSTCRICOID CARCINOMA (SCC). Requires iron supplementation, endoscopic dilation of web, and long-term surveillance endoscopy. Option A: Zenker's diverticulum = pharyngeal pouch at Killian's dehiscence (posterior pharyngeal wall), elderly males, gurgling noise, regurgitation of undigested food, halitosis — no web. Option C: Achalasia = failure of LES relaxation, bird's beak on barium swallow. Option D: Globus pharyngeus = sensation of lump in throat without web or organic cause — no dysphagia to solids, no malignant potential. PEARL: Plummer-Vinson = iron deficiency is the cause, not consequence — treat the iron deficiency and web often resolves.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 5-year-old child with profound bilateral SNHL (>90 dB HL) identified at birth has been using bilateral hearing aids with minimal benefit for 18 months. He has no other comorbidities, cochlear anatomy is normal on MRI, and auditory nerve is intact. Parents are keen on cochlear implantation. Which statement about cochlear implantation in this child is MOST accurate?

options.A: Cochlear implantation should be delayed until after 10 years of age when the cochlea is fully mature
options.B: Unilateral implantation only is the standard, as bilateral implantation doubles risk without benefit
options.C: Early cochlear implantation (before 3.5 years, ideally by 12 months) provides the best speech and language outcomes due to critical period of auditory development
options.D: Children with profound SNHL have intact cochlear hair cells; the implant bypasses the outer hair cells only

questions.explanation: Cochlear implant (CI) candidacy for children: Profound bilateral SNHL + inadequate benefit from hearing aids for 3–6 months = cochlear implant candidate. Critical period of auditory cortex development (0–3 years, especially 0–12 months). Earlier implantation = better auditory cortex maturation, speech perception, and language development. Current guidelines: implant by 12 months if possible for congenital deafness. Maximum benefit window closes progressively after 3.5 years. Option A: Waiting until 10 years = severe language deprivation — contraindicated for congenital profound SNHL. Option B: Bilateral cochlear implantation is now standard of care for children — improves sound localization and speech in noise. Option D: CI bypasses ALL cochlear hair cells (non-functional) and directly electrically stimulates the cochlear nerve (spiral ganglion). PEARL: CI contraindications: absence/aplasia of cochlear nerve (on MRI), cochlear ossification (relative), Michel deformity (complete cochlear agenesis).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 25-year-old woman undergoes elective rhinoplasty for cosmetic improvement. On day 3 post-surgery, she develops severe nasal pain, high fever (39°C), and a red, tense, fluctuant swelling over the nasal dorsum. She is systemically unwell. What is the MOST likely diagnosis and immediate action?

options.A: Haematoma — aspiration in clinic under local anaesthesia
options.B: Septal haematoma — immediate drainage to prevent cartilage avascular necrosis
options.C: Nasal abscess — admission, IV antibiotics, surgical drainage
options.D: Cavernous sinus thrombosis — IV anticoagulation and IV antibiotics

questions.explanation: Post-rhinoplasty nasal abscess (day 3, fever, fluctuant, systemically unwell): Requires IV antibiotics (anti-staphylococcal: flucloxacillin/vancomycin) and surgical drainage under GA. Nasal skin has dangerous area connection to cavernous sinus via facial vein → angular vein → ophthalmic veins → cavernous sinus (valveless veins). Risk of cavernous sinus thrombosis if inadequately treated. Option A: Haematoma = earlier (day 1), no fever, fluctuant but not infected — aspiration is appropriate for haematoma, but infection here requires formal drainage. Option B: Septal haematoma = blood between septal cartilage and perichondrium → purple fluctuant septal swelling bilaterally → avascular necrosis of cartilage → saddle nose deformity if untreated. This is dorsal, not septal. Option D: Cavernous sinus thrombosis presents with proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, papilloedema — not yet present here. PEARL: Danger triangle of face: upper lip to bilateral inner canthi — infections here must be treated aggressively (no squeezing) due to cavernous sinus risk.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 50-year-old woman undergoes total thyroidectomy for multinodular goitre. On post-operative day 1, she develops hoarseness and a breathy voice. Flexible laryngoscopy shows the right vocal cord is paramedian/intermediate position and immobile. Left cord moves normally and compensates partially. Which nerve was injured, and what is the EXPECTED natural course?

options.A: External branch of superior laryngeal nerve — recovers fully within 6 weeks
options.B: Right recurrent laryngeal nerve — with neuropraxia (traction injury), 80–90% recover function within 3–6 months
options.C: Right hypoglossal nerve — causes tongue deviation and articulation problems
options.D: Ansa cervicalis nerve — causes strap muscle weakness with minimal voice change

questions.explanation: Right RLN injury post-thyroidectomy: Hoarseness (breathy voice) + right cord paralysis in paramedian/intermediate position = RLN (not SLN). RLN innervates all intrinsic laryngeal muscles EXCEPT cricothyroid (innervated by external SLN). Neuropraxia (traction/thermal injury without nerve division) = most common intraoperative injury → 80–90% recover within 3–6 months. If nerve was transected (divided) = permanent palsy. Management: Voice therapy, wait 12 months for possible recovery, then surgical medialization (thyroplasty type I/vocal cord augmentation) if no recovery. Option A: External SLN injury = loss of cricothyroid (pitch raising) → monotone voice, loss of high pitch — NOT cord paralysis. Option C: Hypoglossal = tongue movement. Option D: Ansa cervicalis = strap muscle reinnervation used in laryngeal reinnervation procedures. PEARL: Bilateral RLN injury post-thyroidectomy = abductor paralysis, both cords in midline, STRIDOR and airway emergency → emergency tracheostomy.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 45-year-old man presents following acute otitis media with deep retro-orbital eye pain, diplopia with medial deviation of the right eye (abducens palsy), and persistent ear discharge. He has no meningeal signs. MRI shows right petrous apex inflammation with enhancement. What is this syndrome, and what is the involved nerve?

options.A: Ramsay Hunt syndrome — CN VII (geniculate ganglion)
options.B: Gradenigo syndrome — CN VI (abducens nerve) compressed at Dorello's canal at petrous apex
options.C: Vernet syndrome — CN IX, X, XI at jugular foramen
options.D: Collet-Sicard syndrome — CN IX, X, XI, XII at retropharyngeal space

questions.explanation: Gradenigo syndrome (petrous apicitis): Classic triad = (1) Otitis media/ear discharge (2) Retro-orbital/periorbital deep pain (CN V2 — Gasserian ganglion irritation) (3) Abducens nerve palsy (CN VI — ipsilateral lateral rectus palsy, medial deviation of eye/failure of abduction). Pathophysiology: Petrous apex inflammation → spreads to Dorello's canal (fibro-osseous canal through which CN VI traverses at the tip of petrous bone) → compresses CN VI. Treatment: IV antibiotics (anti-pseudomonal), surgical drainage of petrous apex if not resolving. Option A: Ramsay Hunt = VZV + CN VII + cochlear/vestibular signs. Option C: Vernet (jugular foramen syndrome) = IX, X, XI palsy. Option D: Collet-Sicard = IX, X, XI, XII. PEARL: Cranial nerve palsy syndromes at skull base are high-yield NEET PG/INI-CET topics — memorize by location: Jugular foramen (IX, X, XI), Petrous apex/Dorello's canal (VI), Cavernous sinus (III, IV, V1, V2, VI).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A patient with a tracheostomy develops acute severe respiratory distress and cyanosis on post-operative day 4. The tracheostomy tube has become dislodged. Despite attempts to reinsert the tube, it cannot be replaced. The stoma has closed. What is the IMMEDIATE life-saving action?

options.A: Bag-mask ventilation via the mouth and nose while awaiting anaesthetic team
options.B: Cover the stoma and perform mouth-to-nose ventilation
options.C: Oral intubation via the larynx while keeping the stoma patent
options.D: Emergency needle cricothyrotomy through the tracheal stoma or via cricothyroid membrane

questions.explanation: Dislodged tracheostomy tube — EMERGENCY: (1) Call for help (2) Attempt to reinsert tracheostomy tube or a smaller tube/suction catheter to keep stoma open (3) If unable to reinsert → ORAL INTUBATION via larynx (normal route) — most tracheostomy patients can still be intubated orally if larynx intact. (4) If oral intubation fails AND stoma closed → needle/surgical cricothyrotomy. Option A: Bag-mask ventilation via mouth/nose is appropriate IF the patient had a temporary tracheostomy and upper airway is intact — however if there is a laryngectomy (no laryngeal connection), BMV would be useless. Option B: Covering the stoma — in laryngectomy patients, stoma IS the airway; but in tracheostomy (larynx intact), covering the stoma and ventilating via mouth is an option. PEARL: Distinction critical: TOTAL LARYNGECTOMY = stoma is the ONLY airway; bag-mask via mouth useless. TRACHEOSTOMY = larynx intact; can ventilate orally. All tracheostomy emergency kits should include tracheal dilators, spare tube, and 10 ml syringe.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 50-year-old woman presents with pulsatile tinnitus in the left ear, progressive conductive hearing loss, and a reddish pulsatile mass visible behind an intact tympanic membrane. She has no headache or facial nerve weakness. On auscultation over the mastoid, a bruit is heard. MRI shows a highly vascular mass in the middle ear and jugular foramen with flow voids. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate diagnostic and management approach?

options.A: Biopsy of the pulsatile middle ear mass in clinic as first step
options.B: CT, MRI, angiography for staging; pre-operative embolization followed by surgical resection
options.C: Oral propranolol for 12 weeks to reduce vascularity
options.D: Radiotherapy alone as definitive treatment for all glomus tumours

questions.explanation: Glomus tumour (paraganglioma — glomus tympanicum confined to middle ear vs glomus jugulare involving jugular foramen): Pulsatile tinnitus + conductive HL + red pulsatile middle ear mass ('rising sun sign') + bruit = classic presentation. Management: (1) CT temporal bone + MRI with gadolinium (extent, bone erosion, intracranial extension) + angiography (blood supply, identify dominant feeder — typically ascending pharyngeal artery/ICA branches). (2) Pre-operative embolization (reduces intraoperative blood loss). (3) Surgery (tympanotomy for small glomus tympanicum; infratemporal fossa approach for glomus jugulare). Option A: NEVER biopsy a pulsatile middle ear mass — risk of catastrophic haemorrhage. Option C: Propranolol has no role in glomus tumour management. Option D: Radiotherapy is alternative for inoperable/high-surgical-risk cases or skull base glomus jugulare — NOT universal first-line. PEARL: Bilateral glomus tumours + family history + other paragangliomas = SDH gene mutation (succinate dehydrogenase) — genetic testing indicated.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 65-year-old man presents with complete loss of smell (anosmia) following a road traffic accident involving head injury. There was no nasal trauma. He has no nasal obstruction or sinusitis. Sinonasal endoscopy is normal. MRI brain shows no frontal lobe contusion. The most likely mechanism is:

options.A: Cribriform plate fracture causing tearing of olfactory nerve filaments
options.B: Contrecoup injury to the occipital cortex affecting visual integration of smell
options.C: Temporal lobe haematoma compressing the amygdala
options.D: Shearing of olfactory nerve filaments at the cribriform plate due to brain inertia (contre-coup mechanism)

questions.explanation: Post-traumatic anosmia without nasal trauma: The olfactory nerve filaments (fila olfactoria — unmyelinated axons of olfactory receptor neurons) pass through the cribriform plate perforations to synapse in the olfactory bulb. In head injury, sudden deceleration causes relative movement of the brain within the skull → shearing of delicate olfactory filaments at the cribriform plate, even WITHOUT fracture. This is the most common mechanism of post-traumatic anosmia. Option A: Cribriform plate fracture CAN cause anosmia, but is not the mechanism when fracture is absent on imaging. Option B: Occipital cortex = visual cortex (vision, not smell). Option C: Amygdala is involved in smell perception but temporal haematoma is a specific diagnosis not supported here. PEARL: Post-traumatic anosmia recovery: ~30–40% show some improvement. No proven treatment. Olfactory training may help. Associated with CSF rhinorrhoea (cribriform plate defect) — check beta-2 transferrin.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 2-year-old child presents with a barking (seal-like) cough, inspiratory stridor, and mild respiratory distress worsening at night. He had an upper respiratory infection 2 days ago. Temperature is 37.8°C. AP neck X-ray shows a 'steeple sign'. Oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. What is the MOST appropriate initial management for mild-moderate croup?

options.A: IV ceftriaxone to cover bacterial superinfection
options.B: Single dose of oral dexamethasone (0.15–0.6 mg/kg) and supportive care
options.C: Nebulized salbutamol for bronchospasm
options.D: Immediate intubation and ICU admission

questions.explanation: Viral croup (acute laryngotracheobronchitis): Commonest cause = Parainfluenza virus type 1. Barking cough + inspiratory stridor + steeple sign (subglottic narrowing on AP neck X-ray). Mild-moderate (no cyanosis, SaO2 >95%, no significant recession): Single dose dexamethasone (oral 0.15 mg/kg to 0.6 mg/kg) reduces mucosal oedema, decreases hospitalization, reduces duration of stridor. Nebulized epinephrine/adrenaline for moderate-severe (immediate benefit, 2-hour observation post-nebulization for rebound). Option A: Croup is VIRAL — antibiotics not indicated unless bacterial superinfection. Option C: Salbutamol = bronchodilator for lower airway bronchospasm — not indicated for upper airway (subglottic) oedema. Option D: Intubation reserved for severe/impending respiratory failure (SaO2 <92%, severe recession, exhaustion) — not for mild-moderate. PEARL: Croup = inspiratory stridor + steeple sign. Epiglottitis = thumbprint sign. Bacterial tracheitis = Staph aureus, toxic, irregular tracheal narrowing, pseudomembranes.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 35-year-old diabetic presents with fever, severe neck pain, odynophagia, neck rigidity, and painful neck swelling. CT neck with contrast shows a rim-enhancing fluid collection in the retropharyngeal space extending into the superior mediastinum (thoracic inlet). Blood cultures grow Streptococcus milleri. He is systemically septic. What is the MOST life-threatening complication and appropriate management?

options.A: Parapharyngeal abscess — needle aspiration under ultrasound guidance
options.B: Descending necrotising mediastinitis — emergency surgical drainage via transcervical ± thoracotomy + broad-spectrum IV antibiotics
options.C: Ludwig's angina — floor-of-mouth incision and drainage
options.D: Lemierre syndrome — IV benzylpenicillin alone for 4 weeks

questions.explanation: Descending Necrotising Mediastinitis (DNM): Retropharyngeal/parapharyngeal space infection → extends along fascial planes → posterior mediastinum. MOST FEARED complication of deep neck infections. Mortality 25–40%. Aerobes + anaerobes (Streptococcus milleri, Peptostreptococcus, Fusobacterium). CT: neck + chest — shows mediastinal involvement. Management: Emergency surgical drainage (transcervical + thoracotomy if below carina), broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam/metronidazole/antifungals in diabetics), ICU, airway management. Option A: Needle aspiration inadequate for mediastinal spread with sepsis. Option C: Ludwig's angina = submandibular/sublingual space infection (dental origin), floor of mouth swelling — different diagnosis. Option D: Lemierre syndrome = Fusobacterium necrophorum → septic thrombophlebitis of internal jugular vein → septic pulmonary emboli — treatment is IV antibiotics + anticoagulation (controversial). PEARL: CT chest is mandatory for retropharyngeal abscess to rule out DNM — never miss this diagnosis.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 42-year-old woman presents with bilateral high-pitched continuous tinnitus for 18 months following prolonged NSAID (aspirin) use for rheumatoid arthritis. She has no hearing loss on audiogram. She finds the tinnitus most distressing at night. What is the MOST evidence-based management approach?

options.A: Masking with white noise devices alone is curative in most patients
options.B: Tinnitus Retraining Therapy (TRT) — combination of sound therapy (masking/enrichment) and directive counselling
options.C: Antidepressants (amitriptyline) are first-line and most effective treatment
options.D: Ginkgo biloba supplementation — strong evidence for tinnitus reduction

questions.explanation: Tinnitus management: Most tinnitus (subjective, no hearing loss) has no curable cause. TRT (Tinnitus Retraining Therapy) based on Jastreboff's neurophysiological model: habituation to tinnitus signal via (1) sound therapy (partial masking/enrichment, not complete masking) + (2) directive counselling (demystify tinnitus, reduce negative emotional response). Combination is more effective than either alone. Option A: Complete masking (sound that covers tinnitus) may provide temporary relief but does NOT habituate — TRT uses partial masking to allow habituation. Option C: Antidepressants help with tinnitus-related depression/anxiety but are NOT first-line specific treatment; no direct tinnitus reduction evidence. Option D: Cochrane reviews show NO consistent evidence for Ginkgo biloba in tinnitus. PEARL: Aspirin causes bilateral high-frequency tinnitus + SNHL at toxic doses (>6 g/day) via salicylate inhibition of outer hair cell electromotility (reversible). Drug-induced tinnitus — stop the offending drug when possible.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 15-year-old boy presents with progressive unilateral nasal obstruction, massive recurrent epistaxis, and a reddish fleshy mass visible in the nasopharynx. CT shows a highly vascular mass at the sphenopalatine foramen, bowing of the posterior antral wall (Holman Miller sign/antral sign). MRI shows flow voids within the mass. The mass extends into the pterygopalatine fossa. Which of the following statements is MOST accurate?

options.A: Incisional biopsy should be performed to confirm diagnosis before any treatment
options.B: It is a true neoplasm with malignant potential; chemotherapy is required
options.C: Pre-operative embolization followed by surgical resection (endoscopic or open) is the treatment of choice; biopsy is contraindicated due to bleeding risk
options.D: Radiotherapy is the first-line curative treatment for all stages

questions.explanation: Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA): Benign but locally aggressive vascular tumour occurring EXCLUSIVELY in adolescent males. Origin: sphenopalatine foramen region. Holman Miller sign = anterior bowing of posterior antral wall on imaging = pathognomonic. Treatment: Pre-operative embolization (reduces intraoperative blood loss by 50–75%) → surgical excision (endoscopic for small/early stage, open — midfacial degloving/infratemporal fossa approach for advanced). Option A: Biopsy is ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED — risk of life-threatening haemorrhage from this highly vascular tumour. Option B: Benign tumour, no malignant potential — chemotherapy not indicated. Option D: Radiotherapy is reserved for inoperable/recurrent cases (risk of radiation-induced malignancy in young patients). PEARL: Staging: Andrews/Sessions classification. Recurrence rate 15–35%. Testosterone receptors present — may partially regress post-puberty (rarely relied upon). Blood supply: internal maxillary artery (ECA territory) ± ICA feeders.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 30-year-old man sustains a high-speed motor vehicle accident and presents with bilateral periorbital ecchymosis ('raccoon eyes'), flattened midface, CSF rhinorrhoea, and malocclusion (dish-face deformity).
