CT face shows bilateral fractures through the pterygoid plates, zygomatic arches, orbital rims, and nasofrontal suture, separating the entire central facial skeleton from the cranial base. What type of fracture is this?

options.A: Le Fort I fracture — separation of palate from maxilla above the teeth
options.B: Le Fort II fracture — pyramidal fracture through nasal bones and maxilla
options.C: Le Fort III fracture — craniofacial dysjunction, complete separation of facial skeleton from skull base
options.D: Zygomaticomaxillary complex (ZMC) fracture — tripod fracture of the zygomatic complex

questions.explanation: Le Fort fracture classification (René Le Fort, 1901): Le Fort I = Horizontal fracture above the teeth (maxilla only, floating palate, no orbital involvement). Le Fort II = Pyramidal fracture through nasal bones, medial orbital walls, infraorbital rims, and pterygoid plates (nose + maxilla float). Le Fort III = Craniofacial dysjunction: fracture through nasofrontal suture, zygomatic arches, lateral orbital walls, and pterygoid plates → entire face separates from skull (dish-face, raccoon eyes, malocclusion, CSF rhinorrhoea). Option A: Le Fort I = below nasal floor. Option B: Le Fort II = medial/pyramid involving nasal bones but NOT zygomatic arches. Option D: ZMC/tripod fracture = zygomatic arch + zygomaticofrontal suture + infraorbital rim + lateral orbital wall — unilateral. PEARL: All Le Fort fractures pass through the pterygoid plates — this is the key shared anatomical feature (bilateral pterygoid plate fractures = Le Fort fracture).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 5-year-old child is brought by parents complaining of mouth breathing, snoring, nasal speech (hyponasality), recurrent ear infections, and behavioural problems at school. On examination, the child has an open-mouth appearance, 'adenoid facies', and bilateral conductive hearing loss. Lateral neck X-ray shows adenoid pad significantly encroaching on the nasopharyngeal airway. What is the MOST appropriate surgical management?

options.A: Tonsillectomy alone — tonsils are the primary cause of obstruction
options.B: Adenoidectomy ± bilateral grommet insertion for the otitis media with effusion
options.C: CPAP therapy is the gold standard for all paediatric airway obstruction
options.D: Watchful waiting until puberty when adenoids naturally regress

questions.explanation: Adenoid hypertrophy: Nasopharyngeal obstruction → mouth breathing, hyponasal voice, snoring, sleep-disordered breathing, Eustachian tube dysfunction → recurrent OME → conductive hearing loss. 'Adenoid facies' = open mouth, high arched palate, elongated face (chronic mouth breathing alters facial growth). Management: Adenoidectomy (removes obstructing pad) ± grommet insertion (for OME with HL — evidence supports adding grommets if bilateral OME present). Option A: Tonsillectomy alone does not address adenoid pad. Combined adenotonsillectomy if tonsils also enlarged and contributing. Option C: CPAP is for obstructive sleep apnoea in older patients not amenable to surgery — not primary for children with adenoid hypertrophy. Option D: Waiting risks: orthodontic deformity, hearing loss, educational impact, sleep deprivation — intervention indicated. PEARL: Adenoidectomy approach = classic (curettage) or powered microdebrider (more complete). Adenoids regress naturally around puberty but waiting causes harm in symptomatic children.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 10-year-old child with a 3-week history of left ear discharge develops severe headache, high fever, vomiting, and neck stiffness. On examination, Kernig's sign and Brudzinski's sign are positive. CT brain shows diffuse cerebral oedema with no focal abscess. Lumbar puncture shows raised opening pressure, neutrophilic pleocytosis (WBC 2000 cells/µL, 90% neutrophils), protein 180 mg/dL, glucose 20 mg/dL (blood glucose 80 mg/dL). What is the diagnosis and MOST appropriate management sequence?

options.A: Viral meningitis — IV acyclovir and supportive care; LP result confirms viral aetiology
options.B: Bacterial meningitis secondary to otitis media — IV ceftriaxone + dexamethasone, then urgent mastoid surgery after stabilisation
options.C: Lateral sinus thrombosis — IV heparin first, then mastoidectomy
options.D: Brain abscess — IV metronidazole + phenytoin for 4 weeks before considering surgery

questions.explanation: Otogenic bacterial meningitis: Complication of OM/mastoiditis → spread to meninges. CSF: neutrophilic pleocytosis + elevated protein + low glucose (glucose ratio <0.5 = bacterial). Meningeal signs: Kernig's + Brudzinski's positive. Management: (1) IV third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone) immediately — even before CT if no papilloedema/focal signs; (2) IV dexamethasone (reduces hearing loss and mortality in bacterial meningitis — most evidence for Strep pneumoniae); (3) After stabilization → mastoidectomy to eradicate the source (otitis media/mastoiditis). Option A: LP findings (neutrophilic, low glucose, high protein) = BACTERIAL — NOT viral. Viral: lymphocytic, normal glucose, mildly elevated protein. Option C: Lateral sinus thrombosis: headache, fever, Griesinger's sign (oedema over mastoid), raised ICP — LP shows raised pressure, CSF may be normal. Anticoagulation use is controversial. Option D: Brain abscess = CT shows ring-enhancing lesion — not present here. PEARL: Never delay IV antibiotics for LP or CT if bacterial meningitis is strongly suspected and patient is deteriorating.
